verses.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the assembly of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort;
who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
For as the sufferings of Christ abound to us, even so our comfort also abounds through Christ.
But if we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which produces in you the patient enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer.
Our hope for you is steadfast, knowing that, since you are partakers of the sufferings, so also are you of the comfort.

For we don’t desire to have you uninformed, brothers,  concerning our affliction which happened to us in Asia, that we were weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power, so much that we despaired even of life.
Yes, we ourselves have had the sentence of death within ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead,
who delivered us out of so great a death, and does deliver; on whom we have set our hope that he will also still deliver us;
you also helping together on our behalf by your supplication; that, for the gift given to us by means of many, thanks may be given by many persons on your behalf.

For our boasting is this: the testimony of our conscience, that in holiness and sincerity of God, not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God we behaved ourselves in the world, and more abundantly toward you.
For we write no other things to you, than what you read or even acknowledge, and I hope you will acknowledge to the end;
as also you acknowledged us in part, that we are your boasting, even as you also are ours, in the day of our Lord Jesus.
In this confidence, I was determined to come first to you, that you might have a second benefit;
and by you to pass into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you, and to be sent forward by you on my journey to Judea.
When I therefore was thus determined, did I show fickleness? Or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be the “Yes, yes” and the “No, no?”
But as God is faithful, our word toward you was not “Yes and no.”
For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, by me, Silvanus, and Timothy, was not “Yes and no,” but in him is “Yes.”
For however many are the promises of God, in him is the “Yes.” Therefore also through him is the “Amen”, to the glory of God through us.
Now he who establishes us with you in Christ, and anointed us, is God;
who also sealed us, and gave us the down payment of the Spirit in our hearts.
But I call God for a witness to my soul, that I didn’t come to Corinth to spare you.
Not that we control your faith, but are fellow workers with you for your joy. For you stand firm in faith.

footnotes.content: Paul opens with his foundation: not self-appointed, but called by God's will and standing alongside Timothy as a true brother. The letter reaches not just Corinth but all the saints across Achaia—the whole community is in view, not just the troubled ones.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Grace and peace: the cure for a divided church. From God the Father and from Jesus—no distance between them, no bargaining. This is always his first gift, before any correction or wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is why Paul opens with blessing rather than rebuke: because God is the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort. Before addressing their failings, he reminds them—and himself—of God's true character.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God does not comfort us for comfort's sake, but so that we become channels of it to others. Our trials are not wasted—they train us in tenderness. Notice how suffering and consolation flow in the same direction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The sufferings of Christ abound to us"—a paradox that young faith finds hard to swallow. Yet Paul sees his trials as an overflow, even an abundance, of Christ's own afflictions. The same Jesus who was crushed for us still walks the way of difficulty, and his comfort keeps pace with it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Affliction and comfort both have an outward movement: they produce patient endurance in those who watch and are comforted by the apostle's faith. Your faith is not private; it teaches others how to suffer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's hope for them is "steadfast"—not a wish, but a sure knowledge grounded in a shared truth: those who suffer with Christ also receive his comfort with him. Solidarity in sorrow makes room for hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul is candid: something happened in Asia that nearly broke him. To be "weighed down exceedingly" is not weakness to hide; it is the prelude to a miracle. He does not diminish the trial to make the faith look easier.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The sentence of death within ourselves." What sounds like despair is actually grace: stripped of reliance on our own strength, we learn to trust God who raises the dead. Sometimes we have to feel the bottom to find solid ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Past deliverance, present deliverance, future deliverance: God's rescue is not a one-time event but a continuing work. Paul testifies to an active hope, not mere memory—the God who delivers us still does, and will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prayer for an apostle's deliverance becomes a gift that multiplies through many hands. When believers intercede, thanksgiving rises back through many mouths—the community becomes a circuit of grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's boasting is not in eloquence or power but in his conscience—the testimony of walking in "holiness and sincerity" by God's grace, not human wisdom. True strength lies in transparency before God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He writes nothing they have not already read or know in their hearts—the truth is not new, only confirmed. Paul appeals to what they already understand, inviting them to hold to it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the day of judgment, apostle and church will be each other's crown. This mutual honor is not flattery—it is the promise that faithfulness between shepherd and flock is eternal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's plan was to visit them "first"—to prioritize their good. Plans made in love are meant to deliver blessing, a "second benefit" beyond letters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The route through Macedonia to Judea shows Paul's actual journeys—he did not invent plans but traced a hard path, stopping to strengthen churches en route. Geography mattered; so did people on every road.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Did I show fickleness?" Paul's opponents likely used his changed plans as ammunition. He turns it over: is purpose always firm, or does love sometimes require flexibility? The answer traces back to whom we serve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God is faithful—and therefore an apostle sent by God does not speak in contradictions. Even when plans shift, the word remains truthful, not double-minded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesus Christ, preached by Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, is not "Yes and no" but Yes—a single, certain truth in whom all God's promises find their standing. The message has one stable center.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "In him is the Yes. Therefore also through him is the Amen"—a jewel of doctrine. Every promise of God finds its Yes in Christ; believers say Amen to that truth; God receives glory. All of Scripture's hope flows through and ends in Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Established, anointed—God does not leave Paul or Corinth orphaned. He personally secures our standing in Christ, setting us apart as his own. This is the foundation beneath all trust and faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sealed and given the down payment of the Spirit—God has invested his own presence as a pledge. The Spirit in our hearts is not a feeling but a guarantee that God's promises will be completed in us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul calls God as a witness to his motives—a strong oath. He comes not to condemn but because love sometimes requires difficult truth-telling. His sternness with the church flows from tender care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Not that we control your faith, but are fellow workers with you for your joy." Readers today hear an echo in these words: the apostle does not lord it over the flock but stands beside them, both serving their joy and their faith. Authority that serves joy rather than power is the echo we still need to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
